o: We must evaluate a Lisp-like expression string containing integers, variables, `add`, `mult`, and `let` with lexical scoping. The tricky part is scoping: a variable resolves to the value from the innermost enclosing scope, and assignments inside a `let` are sequential and only visible to later parts of that same let. In Example 1, the outer `x=2` is shadowed by the inner `x=3`, so `(mult x ...)` uses 3, giving 3*4=12... wait, the inner let also sets y=4, so it is 3+4=7 times x=2 → 14. Example 2 shows sequential reassignment (`x` ends as 2). Example 3 shows that an assignment expression itself may be a sub-expression evaluated in the current scope. Constraints are tiny (length ≤ 2000), so any correct recursive parse works; we mainly need clean scope handling.
k: Recursive descent over parenthesized expressions naturally mirrors the grammar; each '(' starts a new scope.
Scopes can be modeled as a stack of hash maps; lookup walks the stack from top (innermost) down.

In a `let`, later variables must see earlier assignments of the same let, so all bindings of one let share one scope map; when evaluating the final expr, the last binding's variable should be popped/restored so outer scopes are unaffected.

a.n: Approach 1: Recursion with a global scope stack
a.i: Parse the expression recursively. Maintain a single stack of maps representing active scopes. For `(let v1 e1 ...)`, push one new map, evaluate each ei and record vi sequentially (so later pairs see earlier ones), evaluate the final expression, then pop the map before returning. For `add`/`mult`, just recurse on both operands. Variable lookup scans the stack from the top. This directly encodes lexical scoping and sequential binding.
s: If the expression does not start with '(', it is either an integer or a variable name; return its value via scope lookup or parsing.
Otherwise strip the parentheses and split into tokens at depth 0 by scanning characters (a naive split on spaces fails because sub-expressions contain spaces).
If the head token is 'add'/'mult', recursively evaluate the two remaining tokens and combine.
If 'let': push a new empty scope map; for each (vi, ei) pair evaluate ei in current scopes and set vi; then evaluate the final token, pop the scope, and return the result.
Variable lookup iterates the scope stack from innermost to outermost and returns the first match.
a.t: O(n^2) worst case — each level copies/splits its substring and there can be O(n) nesting levels; fine for n ≤ 2000.
a.sp: O(n) for recursion depth plus scope maps holding at most O(n) total entries.

a.n: Approach 2: Token-stream recursive descent with immutable scope snapshots
a.i: Instead of repeatedly slicing substrings, tokenize once and consume tokens with an index pointer. Each recursive call receives its own copy-on-write view of the environment: pass a list of maps and, on entering a `let`, push a fresh map (and pop after). This avoids quadratic substring copying and makes the parser structure cleaner, closer to how real Lisp interpreters work.
s: Tokenize the whole string once into atoms ('(' , ')', words, numbers).
Use a global index; next() consumes one token.
parse(scopes): if the next token is not '(', handle integer/variable directly.
For add/mult consume '(' implicitly handled by token stream, evaluate two sub-expressions, then expect ')'.
For let: push a new map onto scopes, bind pairs sequentially, evaluate the final expression, pop the map, and return.
a.t: O(n) expected — each token is consumed once and hash lookups are O(1) average per scope level visited.
a.sp: O(n) for the token array, recursion stack, and scope maps.

w: In an interview, Approach 1 is the safest choice: it is short, obviously correct, and n ≤ 2000 makes performance irrelevant. The main pitfalls are (1) splitting on spaces naively — you must track parenthesis depth so nested sub-expressions stay intact; (2) forgetting that within one `let`, later bindings must see earlier ones (use a single shared map per let, not one map per pair); (3) remembering to pop/restore the let's scope after evaluating the body so outer scopes are untouched; (4) handling negative integers when distinguishing numbers from variables. Edge cases: deeply nested lets shadowing the same variable, a let whose final expression is itself another let, and single-token inputs like "3" or "x". Likely follow-ups: extend to division/subtraction, support closures/functions, or evaluate lazily — all build on the same scope-stack idea.
